metadata.title: Amazon to Spend $400M Renovating Two Florida Warehouses, Cut 1,100+ Jobs

content.text:
Amazon is temporarily shutting down two Florida warehouses, laying off 1,100-plus workers and spending $400 million to retrofit both facilities from scratch.
The tech titan expects renovation projects at the Homestead and Port St. Lucie warehouses to take two years to complete.

Earlier this month, Amazon shuttered operations at its 1.3-million-square-foot "TMB8" Homestead facility in Florida, where 616 employees were set to be laid off in two phases. The first batch of cuts took place July 2, while the second set will start Sept. 30.
Amazon also plans on closing its 1-million-square-foot "PBI3" facility in Port St. Lucie, effective Sept. 17, with 494 jobs expected to be cut. The staff reductions will start on the closure date, and then again on Dec. 17.
According to the Worker Adjustment and Rehabilitation Notification (WARN) notices filed in April and July, affected employees who accept internal transfer opportunities at Amazon prior to their separation date will not be laid off.
Both WARN notices indicated that the employee separations are expected to be permanent despite the tentative reopening of both facilities in 2028.
Amazon said about 300 employees had accepted transfers from the Homestead warehouse to other facilities.
The overwhelming majority of the 1,110 employees impacted across the two warehouses are fulfillment center associates who are responsible for picking, packing, stowing and preparing orders for shipment.
The Homestead site is an inbound cross-dock (IXD) facility designed to take in freight from ports and domestic suppliers before distributing products to fulfillment centers. As part of the project, Amazon will convert the site into a full-scale fulfillment center for an estimated $200 million.
Renovation at the Port Lucie warehouse is also expected to cost $200 million. That site hosts, stores and ships large and bulky items like kayaks, patio furniture, grills, gym equipment and other larger household goods. Like it TMB8 counterpart, the PBI3 building will be renovated into a sortable fulfillment center designed to handle smaller items.
Upon their completion, the new facilities are expected to employ roughly 1,000 people each, Amazon says.
Beyond the renovations, Amazon expects to further scale its warehouse footprint in Florida, prepping to build a new 1.1-million-square-foot facility in Fort Pierce that is expected to cost $240 million.
